### keynav for Mac: why it won't run, and the closest grid alternatives

Source: https://nomousemode.com/keynav-for-mac  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

**keynav doesn't run on macOS: its own README says it only works on X11.** If what you miss is narrowing the screen down to a spot in a few keystrokes, Mac apps can do that with a keyboard grid. Here are your options.

> **Short answer:** **keynav can't run on a Mac.** Its README says it "only works on X11", and macOS apps don't use X11. The closest thing on macOS is a keyboard grid that narrows the screen down to the spot you want. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/)'s jump grid does it with a 3×3 grid on `Q` `W` `E` / `A` `S` `D` / `Z` `X` `C`, two or three presses to anywhere. Free options exist too: warpd's grid mode (not updated since 2023), Voice Control's "Show grid" and Mouse Keys, each with trade-offs below.

#### What keynav is, and why it stays on Linux

[keynav](https://github.com/jordansissel/keynav)'s tagline is "retire your mouse": it controls the mouse with the keyboard. It's free and open source, with about 653 stars on GitHub, and its last commit was in August 2022.

The reason you can't brew-install it on a Mac is spelled out in its README: "This project (keynav) only works on X11." The FAQ goes further: keynav is totally dependent on X11, and for macOS it suggests AppleScript instead. It doesn't support Wayland either. X11 is the window system that many Linux desktops use; macOS draws its windows with its own system, so a port isn't a weekend job, it's a rewrite.

The good news is that the idea travels. Mac apps can't reuse keynav's code, but they can do the same kind of thing through macOS's own accessibility and pointer controls.

#### The idea you're probably after: narrow down, don't steer

Most "keyboard mouse" tools make you steer the pointer like a tiny car with arrow keys. Grid tools take a different route. You see the screen split into cells, press the key for the cell your target is in, the grid shrinks into that cell, and you press again. A few keystrokes later the pointer is on the spot. It's fast, it's the same number of keys whether the target is near or far, and it never needs to know what's on screen.

That last point matters on a Mac. Click-label tools (like [Vimium-style labels for the whole Mac](https://nomousemode.com/vimium-for-mac)) depend on apps describing their buttons to macOS. A grid doesn't care, so it works in games, design canvases, remote desktops and anything else.

#### Keyboard grids on macOS, compared

Checked against each tool's own docs in October 2026:

|  | No Mouse Mode jump grid | warpd grid mode | Voice Control grid | Mouse Keys |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| How you narrow down | 3×3 grid, zooms in with each press | Pick quadrants repeatedly with u i j k | Say a grid number; it refines | No grid: steer with keys |
| Keys | Q W E / A S D / Z X C | u i j k | Your voice | 7 8 9 U O J K L |
| Open it | E while No Mouse Mode is on | ⌥⌘G (A-M-g) | "Show grid" | Accessibility setting |
| Click | Space click, Return right-click | m left, , middle, . right | By voice | I click (no right-click key) |
| Works in any app | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Maintained | Yes (2.0.1) | Not updated since 2023 | Built into macOS | Built into macOS |
| Price | $19.99 one time, 1 Mac | Free, MIT | Free | Free |

#### No Mouse Mode's jump grid

Press `⇧⌘M` to turn [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) on, then `E`. The screen with the pointer splits into a 3×3 grid labelled `Q` `W` `E` / `A` `S` `D` / `Z` `X` `C`, the same shape as those keys on your keyboard, so you don't read the labels so much as point with your fingers. Press a letter and the pointer jumps to the middle of that cell, then the grid zooms into it. Two or three presses reach anywhere.

- `Space` clicks there, `Return` right-clicks.
- `Delete` goes back a level if you picked the wrong cell.
- `Tab` moves the grid to your next display; `Esc` closes it.
- Afterwards you can fine-tune with `W` `A` `S` `D` (hold `Q` for one-pixel precision).

The grid is one part of a bigger app. When a target is a real button, `⇧⌘Space` click labels are usually faster: type the letters on it and it's clicked. You also get type to click, scroll areas, saved spots (`Shift+1`–`9` to save, `1`–`9` to jump) and every key can be remapped. It needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later on Apple silicon or Intel.

#### The free options

##### warpd: the closest in spirit, but quiet since 2023

[warpd](https://github.com/rvaiya/warpd) is "a modal keyboard-driven virtual pointer" for X11, Wayland (sway/wlroots) and macOS. Its grid mode (`⌥⌘G`, written A-M-g in its docs) lets you pick quadrants over and over with `u`/`i`/`j`/`k`, then `m`, `,` or `.` to click. If you used keynav on Linux and want something that feels like a Unix tool, it's the natural first try. The catch: its last commit was June 2023 and its last macOS release (v1.3.5) was November 2022, and it doesn't state a minimum macOS. Full details in [warpd for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/warpd-for-mac).

##### Voice Control's "Show grid"

Built into macOS (System Settings > Accessibility > Voice Control). Say "Show grid" for a numbered grid over the screen, or "Show window grid" for just the active window. Say a number to refine it, and "Hide grid" when you're done. It's the same narrowing idea, and free, but you speak rather than type, which isn't for every room.

##### Mouse Keys

Also built in (System Settings > Accessibility > Pointer Control > Mouse Keys). It moves the pointer with `7` `8` `9` `U` `O` `J` `K` `L` (or the keypad) and clicks with `I`. There's no grid, so it's steering rather than narrowing, and Apple notes that while it's on you can't use the keyboard to enter text. It's fine for an emergency; see [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys) for the long version.

##### Two more grid apps

- **[Scoot](https://github.com/mjrusso/scoot)** (free, BSD-3, v1.3 March 2026): a grid mode on `⇧⌘K` with equal cells across all screens, each with a key sequence. Its README says it runs on macOS 11 and 12; newer versions aren't stated.
- **[Mouseless](https://mouseless.click)** (closed source, 14-day trial, prices not published on its site): tap Left Command to show a grid, type a cell's two characters, then Space clicks its center or a sub-grid key picks a sub-cell.

#### Which should you pick?

- **You only need to click now and then:** start with Voice Control or Mouse Keys. They're free and already on your Mac.
- **You want the Unix-tool feel and don't mind risk:** try warpd, knowing it isn't being updated.
- **You want a grid plus click labels, scrolling and remappable keys in one maintained app:** [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/), $19.99 one time for 1 Mac as of October 2026 ([pricing](https://nomousemode.com/#pricing)). There's no free trial, but the live demo on this page uses the same keys.

For the bigger picture, see [how to move the mouse with the keyboard on a Mac](https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac) and [the best keyboard mouse apps for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/best-keyboard-mouse-apps-for-mac).

**Reach any spot on your Mac in three keys.** Press E for a 3×3 grid on Q W E / A S D / Z X C, narrow down, then Space to click, in any app. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### Can I install keynav on macOS?

No. keynav's README says "This project (keynav) only works on X11", and its FAQ says it is totally dependent on X11. macOS doesn't use X11 for its own apps, so there's nothing for keynav to control. There's no Wayland version either.

##### What's the closest thing to keynav on a Mac?

A keyboard grid. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/)'s jump grid (press `E`) splits the screen into a 3×3 grid on Q W E / A S D / Z X C and zooms in with each press. warpd has a grid mode with four quadrants. Voice Control has a numbered grid you control by voice. Scoot and Mouseless also have grid modes.

##### Is there a free keynav alternative for macOS?

Yes. Voice Control and Mouse Keys are built into macOS and free. warpd (MIT) and Scoot (BSD-3) are free and open source, though warpd hasn't been updated since 2023 and Scoot's README only states macOS 11 and 12. No Mouse Mode is paid: $19.99 one time for 1 Mac as of October 2026.

##### Can I click and right-click from the grid?

In No Mouse Mode, yes: after narrowing down, press `Space` to click or `Return` to right-click. `Delete` goes back a level, `Tab` moves the grid to your next display and `Esc` closes it. You can still fine-tune with W A S D afterwards. In warpd's grid mode, `m`, `,` and `.` are left, middle and right click.

##### Does the jump grid work in every app?

Yes. The grid doesn't need to know where an app's buttons are; it just moves the pointer to a spot on screen. That's why it works in games, design canvases and remote desktops where click labels can't see anything.

##### Does it work with several displays?

Yes. The grid appears on the display the pointer is on, and `Tab` moves it to the next one. Outside the grid, `Tab` and `Shift+Tab` jump the pointer between displays.

### Mac trackpad or mouse not working? What to do, using only the keyboard

Source: https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

A dead pointer feels like a locked door, but your keyboard can still do almost everything. **Start with Apple's quick fixes, then use the built-in keyboard tools to keep working** while you sort out the hardware.

> **Short answer:** Don't panic: you can do this from the keyboard. If it's a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad, press `⌘Space`, type **Bluetooth File Exchange**, press `Return`, then `Return` again to turn Bluetooth on. Then switch the device off and on, restart if Bluetooth won't come on, or plug it in by cable for a minute. To keep working meanwhile, press `⌥⌘F5` and turn on Mouse Keys, which moves the pointer from the keyboard. If it's the MacBook's own trackpad and nothing helps, contact [Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/contact).

#### First, a few keys that help right now

Before you fix anything, it helps to know how to get around. These all work with no pointer at all:

| Press | What it does |
|---|---|
| ⌘Space | Opens Spotlight search. Type an app's name and press Return to open it |
| ⌘Tab | Switches between open apps |
| ⌥⌘F5 | Opens the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, where you can turn on Mouse Keys |
| Control-F2 | Puts focus on the menu bar (arrows to move, Return to choose) |
| Control-F3 | Puts focus on the Dock |

If a Control-F key does nothing, add `Fn` (for example `Fn-Control-F2`). Apple says some of these shortcuts must first be switched on in System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Keyboard.

#### Step 1: Apple's quick fixes for a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad

These come from Apple's support article, [If your Bluetooth mouse, keyboard or trackpad isn't working](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102498). Go in order and stop when it works.

1. **Turn Bluetooth on without a mouse.** Press `⌘Space`, type **Bluetooth File Exchange** and press `Return`. Press `Return` again to turn Bluetooth on.
2. **Turn the device off and on.** The switch shows green when it's on.
3. **Check Bluetooth in System Settings.** Make sure it's switched on.
4. **Restart** if Bluetooth won't turn on.
5. **Connect by cable for one minute**, then unplug it. This pairs the device and charges it at the same time. A flat battery is an easy thing to miss.
6. **Think about interference.** Apple notes that wireless interference can cause drop-outs.

#### Step 2: If it's the MacBook's built-in trackpad

Apple's article above is about Bluetooth devices, so most of it doesn't apply to the trackpad built into a MacBook. A restart is still worth a try. If the trackpad is jumpy or clicking on its own, Mouse Keys has an option to **ignore the built-in trackpad** while it's on (more on that below), which can stop it getting in your way. Beyond that, a built-in trackpad that doesn't work is a job for [Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/contact).

#### Step 3: Keep working with what's built in

Your Mac has three free tools that work without any pointer device. You may need only one of them.

##### Mouse Keys: move the pointer with the keyboard

Press `⌥⌘F5` to open the Accessibility Shortcuts panel and turn on Mouse Keys, or go to System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control → Mouse Keys. Then:

- `7` `8` `9` `U` `O` `J` `K` `L` move the pointer (or the numeric keypad, if you have one).
- `I` clicks (keypad `5`). `M` presses and holds, `.` releases.

Two catches: while Mouse Keys is on, **you can't type text** with those keys, and Apple's Mouse Keys page lists no right-click key. Its options (the info button next to Mouse Keys) include "Press the Option key five times to toggle Mouse Keys", "Ignore built-in trackpad when Mouse Keys is on", and the pointer's speed. Our [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys) page goes deeper.

##### Full Keyboard Access: Tab to buttons

Turn it on in System Settings → Accessibility → Motor → Keyboard. Then `Tab` moves a highlight between items and `Space` selects. It's great for dialogs and settings screens. Full details in our [Full Keyboard Access guide](https://nomousemode.com/full-keyboard-access-mac).

##### Voice Control: click by speaking

Turn it on in System Settings → Accessibility → Voice Control. Say **"Show numbers"** to put a number on each item, then **"Click"** and the number. "Show grid" gives you a numbered grid for clicking anywhere, and "Hide numbers" or "Hide grid" removes them.

#### Which built-in tool for which job?

| You need to… | Built-in option | No Mouse Mode (if already set up) |
|---|---|---|
| Open an app | ⌘Space, type its name | Same, or click its label in the Dock |
| Press a button | Full Keyboard Access: Tab until you reach it, then Space | ⇧⌘Space, type its label |
| Click a spot that isn't a button | Mouse Keys, or Voice Control's grid | Jump grid (E) or W A S D |
| Right-click | Alternate pointer actions, or Voice Control | Return |
| Scroll | Arrow keys inside many apps' lists and pages | Arrow keys, or scroll areas (⇧⌘J) |
| Drag | Mouse Keys: M to hold, move, . to release | Hold Space and move |
| Type | Turn Mouse Keys off first | Turns itself off when you click into a text box |

#### Keep working with No Mouse Mode

If you'd rather not juggle three accessibility features, [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) turns the keyboard into a full mouse. Press `⇧⌘Space` to label every button, link and menu (plus the menu bar and the Dock) and type a label to click it. Or press `⇧⌘M` and glide the pointer with `W` `A` `S` `D`: `Space` clicks, `Return` right-clicks, hold `Space` to drag, and the arrow keys scroll. Shortcuts with Command, Control or Option still go straight to your apps.

Be realistic about two things:

- **You need to be able to install it.** Setup normally means dragging the app into Applications, then switching on the Accessibility permission in System Settings. We haven't documented doing that with the keyboard alone, so we don't promise it. The easy way round it: borrow any wired mouse for a few minutes, or better, set it up now while your pointer still works.
- **It's paid, with no free trial.** $19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, as of October 2026 ([see pricing](https://nomousemode.com/#pricing)). You can try the same keys in the demo on this page first. It needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. If you only need to get through a day or two, the free built-ins above may be plenty.

Once it's set up, it doesn't need a mouse or trackpad at all, and it doesn't fix hardware either: it just means a broken trackpad doesn't stop your work. New to it? Open Practice from the menu bar icon for nine short lessons, or press `H` while it's on to see every key. Questions are answered on the [support page](https://nomousemode.com/support).

#### When to call Apple

Contact [Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/contact) if:

- a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad still won't connect after the steps above, even after charging it by cable;
- the built-in MacBook trackpad doesn't respond, or keeps clicking or moving on its own after a restart.

Until then, your keyboard has you covered. For the full picture of working without a pointer, read our [guide to using a Mac without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/how-to-use-mac-without-mouse).

**Be ready for the next time** Set up No Mouse Mode while your pointer works, and a dead trackpad or a flat mouse battery won't stop your day. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### How do I turn on Bluetooth on a Mac without a mouse?

Apple's tip: press Command-Space bar, type "Bluetooth File Exchange", press Return, then press Return again to turn Bluetooth on. Your Bluetooth mouse or trackpad can then reconnect.

##### My Bluetooth mouse or Magic Trackpad stopped working. What should I try first?

Turn the device off and on again (the switch shows green when it's on). Check that Bluetooth is on in System Settings. If Bluetooth won't turn on, restart the Mac. If the device can use a cable, connect it for one minute and then unplug it: that pairs and charges it. Wireless interference can also cause drop-outs. These steps come from Apple's own [support article](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102498).

##### How do I move the pointer with the keyboard on a Mac?

Turn on Mouse Keys: press Option-Command-F5 to open the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, or go to System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control → Mouse Keys. Then 7 8 9 U O J K L move the pointer and I clicks. You can't type text while Mouse Keys is on. More in [how to move the mouse with the keyboard](https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac).

##### How do I right-click without a mouse or trackpad?

Built in, you can turn on Alternate pointer actions (System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control), or use Voice Control. Some Apple keyboards with a numeric keypad have a Contextual Menu key. In No Mouse Mode, Return right-clicks. See [how to right-click without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/right-click-without-mouse-mac).

##### My MacBook's built-in trackpad is jumpy or clicking by itself. Can I ignore it?

Mouse Keys has an option called "Ignore built-in trackpad when Mouse Keys is on" (click the info button next to Mouse Keys). For a built-in trackpad that keeps misbehaving, contact [Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/contact), because it may need a repair.

##### Can I install No Mouse Mode without a mouse?

We haven't documented a keyboard-only install, so we don't promise one. Setup normally means dragging the app into Applications and switching on the Accessibility permission. The safest plan is to install it while your pointer works, or borrow any wired mouse for a few minutes. Once it's set up, it works with no mouse or trackpad at all.

##### Does No Mouse Mode fix a broken trackpad?

No. It doesn't repair hardware. It lets you move, click, scroll and drag from the keyboard, so you can keep working while you wait for a fix or a replacement.

### How to move the mouse with the keyboard on a Mac

Source: https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

**Turn on Mouse Keys and use 7 8 9 U O J K L to move the pointer and I to click**, or use an app like No Mouse Mode to steer it with W A S D. Here's how both work and when each one is enough.

> **Short answer:** macOS has this built in: turn on **Mouse Keys** in System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control, then **7 8 9 U O J K L** move the pointer and **I** clicks. It's free and fine for a few clicks, but you can't type while it's on and it has no right-click key. If you move the pointer by keyboard every day, [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) steers it with **W A S D**, adds fast and one-pixel modes, a jump grid and saved spots, and gets out of the way when you type.

#### Option 1: Mouse Keys (built in, free)

##### Turn it on

1. Open the Apple menu → System Settings → **Accessibility → Pointer Control**.
2. Switch on **Mouse Keys**.
3. Optional: click the info button next to it for more settings (below).

Shortcut: `⌥⌘F5` (or triple-pressing Touch ID) opens the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, where you can turn Mouse Keys on or off.

##### The keys

| Action | Keyboard | Numeric keypad |
|---|---|---|
| Move (eight directions) | 7 8 9 U O J K L | 7 8 9 4 6 1 2 3 |
| Click | I | 5 |
| Press and hold (start a drag) | M | 0 |
| Release | . | . |

So 8 is up, K is down, U is left and O is right, with 7, 9, J and L for the diagonals. I sits in the middle as the click.

##### Settings worth changing

- **Press the Option key five times to toggle Mouse Keys.** Turn this on. You'll be switching it on and off a lot.
- **Initial delay** and **Maximum speed**: how long before the pointer starts to speed up, and how fast it gets.
- **Ignore built-in trackpad when Mouse Keys is on**: handy if a faulty trackpad is making the pointer jump.

##### Its limits

Apple is direct about the big one: "When Mouse Keys is on, you can't use the keyboard or numeric keypad to enter text." Every time you want to type a URL or a message, you toggle it off and back on.

Apple's Mouse Keys page also lists no right-click key. For right, double-click and drag via keyboard shortcuts you turn on **Alternate pointer actions** in the same Pointer Control pane. And there's no way to jump across the screen or to another display: you steer the whole way.

#### Option 2: No Mouse Mode's W A S D pointer

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) uses the keys gamers already know. Press `⇧⌘M` to turn it on (or hold Right Command or Right Option, if you turn on hold-to-use), then:

| Action | Key |
|---|---|
| Move (smooth, eases in, speeds up as you hold) | W A S D |
| Fast | hold Shift |
| Precise, one pixel at a time | hold Q |
| Click (twice: double, three times: triple, hold: drag) | Space |
| Right-click / middle click | Return / M |
| Back / forward buttons | [ / ] |
| Scroll in every direction | arrow keys |
| Jump grid | E |
| Next / previous display | Tab / ⇧Tab |
| Jump to a saved spot / save one | 1–9 / ⇧1–⇧9 |
| Jump back | ` |
| Show every key | H |

Every key can be remapped in Settings, and shortcuts that use Command, Control or Option still reach the app you're in.

##### Jump instead of steering

Long trips are where steering gets tedious. Press `E` and a 3×3 grid labelled Q W E / A S D / Z X C (the same shape as those keys) covers the screen. Press a letter and the pointer jumps to that cell, then the grid zooms in. Two or three presses reach any point, then you fine-tune with W A S D. It works in any app.

For places you visit all the time, like a toolbar button in your editor, press `⇧` and a number to save the spot, and the number alone to jump back to it. ``` returns the pointer to where it was before its last jump.

##### Often you don't need the pointer at all

If the target is a button, link, tab or menu, don't steer to it. Press `⇧⌘Space` and type its label, or `⇧⌘/` and type its name. These work even with No Mouse Mode off. Labels rely on apps describing their buttons to macOS, which most do. The grid and W A S D work everywhere.

#### Side by side

|  | Mouse Keys | No Mouse Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, built in | $19.99 one time, 1 Mac (as of October 2026) |
| Move keys | 7 8 9 U O J K L | W A S D |
| Speed control | Initial delay and max speed settings | Eases in; hold Shift fast, Q precise |
| Right-click key | No (needs Alternate pointer actions) | Yes, Return |
| Scroll | No | Yes, arrow keys |
| Jump across the screen | No | Grid, saved spots, jump back |
| Multiple displays | Steer across | Tab / Shift-Tab |
| Typing | Blocked while on | Turns itself off when you click a text box |
| Click buttons by label | No | Yes |

The full head-to-head is in [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys).

#### When is Mouse Keys enough?

- **Your trackpad broke and a new one arrives tomorrow.** Mouse Keys plus Full Keyboard Access will get you there. See [what to do when your trackpad isn't working](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working).
- **You click a few times a day** and mostly type in between. Toggling with Option five times is fine.
- **You have a numeric keypad** and like using it as a joystick.

#### When you'll want more

- You move the pointer and type in the same minute, all day.
- You right-click, scroll or drag often.
- You have more than one display.
- You're going keyboard-only for comfort. See [using a Mac keyboard-only for wrist pain](https://nomousemode.com/keyboard-only-mac-rsi).

Used tools like warpd or keynav on Linux? [warpd for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/warpd-for-mac) and [keynav for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/keynav-for-mac) cover how they map over. For the bigger picture, start at [how to use a Mac without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/how-to-use-mac-without-mouse), or see [No Mouse Mode pricing](https://nomousemode.com/#pricing).

**Steer your Mac's pointer with W A S D** No Mouse Mode moves the pointer smoothly with fast and pixel-precise modes, a jump grid, saved spots and display jumps. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### How do I turn on Mouse Keys on a Mac?

Open System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control and switch on Mouse Keys. You can also press Option-Command-F5 to open the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, or turn on the option to press Option five times to toggle it.

##### Which keys move the mouse in Mouse Keys?

7, 8, 9, U, O, J, K and L move the pointer (or 7 8 9 4 6 1 2 3 on a numeric keypad). I clicks (keypad 5), M presses and holds (keypad 0), and the period releases.

##### Why can't I type when Mouse Keys is on?

That's how it works. Apple says that when Mouse Keys is on, you can't use the keyboard or numeric keypad to enter text. Turn it off to type, for example by pressing Option five times if you've enabled that option.

##### How do I make Mouse Keys faster?

Click the info button next to Mouse Keys in System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control and adjust Initial delay and Maximum speed.

##### Can I move the mouse with W A S D on a Mac?

Not with macOS alone. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) does it: press Shift-Command-M, then W A S D move the pointer, Shift goes fast, Q goes one pixel at a time, and Space clicks. Every key can be remapped.

##### How do I move the pointer to another display with the keyboard?

In [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/), press Tab for the next display and Shift-Tab for the previous one. Mouse Keys has no display jump, so you steer across.

### Homerow vs No Mouse Mode: which keyboard-clicking app fits you?

Source: https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-homerow  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

Both put letter labels on buttons so you can click with the keyboard. **Homerow focuses on labels, search and scrolling; No Mouse Mode adds a full keyboard mouse on top, for less money on one Mac.**

> **Short answer:** Homerow is a polished, actively maintained app that labels buttons so you can click them by typing, with search and scrolling too. It costs $49.99 once for all your personal Macs and is free to try. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) does click labels, type to click and scroll areas as well, then adds a full keyboard mouse: smooth W A S D movement, every mouse button, a jump grid, saved spots and display jumps. It's $19.99 for one Mac, with no trial but live demos on the site. If you only need labels across several Macs, Homerow is a fair pick. If you want to drop the mouse completely on one or two Macs, No Mouse Mode does more for less.

#### What Homerow does well

[Homerow](https://www.homerow.app) describes itself as "keyboard shortcuts for every button in macOS". You press a shortcut, small labels appear on the buttons, links and other controls on screen, and you type a label to click it. Its site shows three main features: **labels**, **search** and **scroll**.

- **It's mature.** Homerow is the successor of Vimac, the free open-source keyboard navigation app. Vimac's README calls Homerow "a refined, sleeker, more performant successor".
- **It's maintained.** The latest version is 1.5.3, released March 19, 2026, and version 1.1.0 added extra scroll-mode commands.
- **The license is generous.** One $49.99 purchase covers all your personal Macs and all future updates, as of October 2026. There's also a student discount.
- **You can try it first.** Homerow is free to try, with a reminder every 50 activations.
- **It runs on older macOS.** It needs macOS 13 or later.

Homerow says it works with "most native macOS apps and a growing set of non-native web-based apps". That's the honest limit of every label app: labels only appear where an app tells macOS about its buttons.

#### What No Mouse Mode does differently

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) starts from the same idea, then tries to replace the mouse entirely. It has three shortcuts that work anywhere: `⇧⌘Space` for click labels, `⇧⌘/` for type to click and `⇧⌘J` for scroll areas. Press `⇧⌘M` to turn on No Mouse Mode itself, and the keyboard becomes a mouse.

##### Click labels and type to click

Every button, link, tab, menu, the menu bar and the Dock get letter labels. Hold Shift with the last letter to right-click, Command for a Command-click (new tab), Option to double-click, or Control to just move the pointer there. Press Tab to keep labels open for several clicks in a row. Labels for a window stay the same each time, so you build muscle memory. Type to click lets you type part of a button's name instead (initials work), then press Return.

##### A real keyboard mouse

With No Mouse Mode on, `W` `A` `S` `D` move the pointer smoothly, easing in. Hold Shift to go fast or Q for one-pixel precision. Space clicks (twice to double-click, hold to drag), Return right-clicks, M middle-clicks and [ / ] are back and forward. The arrow keys scroll in every direction. This is the part that matters when a control has no label, or when you need to drag, select text or draw.

##### Getting anywhere fast

Press `E` for the jump grid: a 3×3 grid labelled Q W E / A S D / Z X C that zooms in with each press, so two or three presses reach any spot on screen. Save spots with Shift+1–9 and jump back to them with 1–9, press ``` to jump back, and use Tab / Shift+Tab to move between displays.

##### Help for apps that don't cooperate

An optional mode reads on-screen text with Apple's on-device text recognition, so apps that don't describe their buttons to macOS can still get labels. It needs Screen Recording permission, and nothing is saved or sent. Turn it off and No Mouse Mode needs only Accessibility.

##### Built to be learned

A guided first-run setup, a Practice window with nine hands-on lessons, and `H` to show every key. Every key and shortcut can be remapped.

#### Homerow vs No Mouse Mode at a glance

"Not listed" means Homerow's website doesn't mention the feature. It doesn't prove Homerow lacks it, so check its site if that feature matters to you.

|  | Homerow | No Mouse Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Click labels | Yes | Yes, incl. menu bar and Dock |
| Search / type to click | Yes (search) | Yes, initials work |
| Scrolling | Yes (scroll mode) | Yes, scroll areas plus arrow keys |
| W A S D pointer movement | Not listed | Yes, with fast and precise modes |
| Drag, right, middle, back/forward | Not listed | Yes |
| Jump grid | Not listed | Yes, 3×3, works in any app |
| Saved spots | Not listed | Yes, 1–9 |
| Display jumps | Not listed | Yes, Tab / Shift+Tab |
| Practice lessons | Not listed | Yes, nine lessons |
| On-screen text recognition fallback | Not listed | Yes, optional, on-device |
| macOS | 13 or later | 14 Sonoma or later, Apple silicon and Intel |
| Price (Oct 2026) | $49.99 once | $19.99 once (1 Mac) |
| Macs covered | All your personal Macs | 1 Mac; 3 for $49.99, 5 for $79.99, 20 for $299.99 |
| Try before buying | Free to try, reminder every 50 activations | No trial; interactive demos in the browser |
| Updates | All future updates included | Free updates, no subscription |
| Open source | No | No |

#### Price and trial, plainly

As of October 2026, Homerow is **$49.99 once** and covers all your personal Macs. No Mouse Mode is **$19.99 once for one Mac**, $49.99 for three, $79.99 for five and $299.99 for twenty. Neither is a subscription, and both include updates.

- **One Mac:** No Mouse Mode costs $30 less.
- **Three Macs:** the same price.
- **Four or more personal Macs:** Homerow is cheaper.

The try-before-you-buy story is different too. Homerow lets you use the real app for free, with a reminder every 50 activations. No Mouse Mode has **no free trial**, and all sales are final. What it offers instead is the live demo on this page and on the [homepage](https://nomousemode.com/): they run in your browser and use the same keys as the app, so you can feel the labels, the grid and W A S D movement before you pay.

#### The shared limit: apps have to describe their buttons

Both apps find buttons through macOS accessibility information. Most Mac apps and websites provide it. Some apps don't, and there labels may be missing or incomplete. No Mouse Mode's answer is the optional text recognition mode, the jump grid and W A S D movement, which work everywhere because they don't need to know what's on screen. If you mostly live in well-behaved apps, this difference may never come up.

#### Who should pick which

##### Pick Homerow if…

- you mainly want to click buttons and links by typing, and you're happy using a mouse or trackpad for everything else;
- you use four or more personal Macs and want one license for all of them;
- you want to try the real app for a while before you pay;
- you're on macOS 13 Ventura.

##### Pick No Mouse Mode if…

- you want to stop reaching for the mouse altogether, including dragging, right-clicking and precise pointing;
- you hit apps where labels don't show up and want a grid or pointer that always works;
- you use one or two Macs and want the lower price;
- you'd like practice lessons to get fluent quickly, for example if you're [cutting back on the mouse because of wrist pain](https://nomousemode.com/keyboard-only-mac-rsi) or your [trackpad has stopped working](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working).

Already using a free option? Apple's built-in tools may be enough for light use. See [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys), or the full [list of Homerow alternatives](https://nomousemode.com/homerow-alternatives), including Shortcat, Wooshy, Scoot and Mouseless.

#### Can you run both?

You can, but there's little reason to: their label, search and scroll shortcuts look alike. If you do, remap No Mouse Mode's shortcuts in its settings so they don't overlap. For a full walkthrough of keyboard-only use, start with [how to use a Mac without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/how-to-use-mac-without-mouse), and see [support](https://nomousemode.com/support) for setup and permissions.

**Click, move and scroll without touching the mouse** No Mouse Mode is $19.99 once for one Mac, with free updates and no subscription. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### Is Homerow worth it?

If you want click labels, search and scrolling and you use several Macs, Homerow is a well-maintained choice. As of October 2026 it costs $49.99 once, covers all your personal Macs and includes future updates. It's free to try, with a reminder every 50 activations, so you can find out for yourself.

##### Is No Mouse Mode cheaper than Homerow?

For one Mac, yes: $19.99 versus $49.99 (as of October 2026). No Mouse Mode's 3-Mac license is $49.99, the same as Homerow. For four or more Macs, Homerow's single price is cheaper, because it covers all your personal Macs. See [No Mouse Mode pricing](https://nomousemode.com/#pricing).

##### Does No Mouse Mode have a free trial like Homerow?

No. No Mouse Mode has no free trial and all sales are final. Instead, the website has interactive in-browser demos that use the same keys as the app, so you can try the feel before buying. Homerow is free to try, with a reminder every 50 activations.

##### Do Homerow and No Mouse Mode use the same shortcuts?

They look similar. Homerow's website demos show ⌘⇧Space for labels, ⌘⇧J for scroll and ⌘⇧/ for search. No Mouse Mode's defaults are ⇧⌘Space (click labels), ⇧⌘J (scroll areas) and ⇧⌘/ (type to click). Every No Mouse Mode shortcut can be remapped, so you can change them if you run both.

##### Which one works in more apps?

Both rely on apps describing their buttons to macOS. Homerow says it works with most native macOS apps and a growing set of web-based apps. No Mouse Mode has an optional on-device text recognition mode for apps that don't describe their buttons, plus a jump grid and W A S D movement that work in any app.

##### Is Homerow the same as Vimac?

Homerow is Vimac's successor. Vimac's README says "Vimac is now Homerow". The open-source Vimac hasn't been updated since 2022. If you're still on it, see [Vimac alternatives](https://nomousemode.com/vimac-alternative).

##### What macOS versions do they need?

Homerow needs macOS 13 or later. No Mouse Mode needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later and runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

### Mouse Keys on Mac: how to use it, fix it, and when to move on

Source: https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

Mouse Keys is the free mouse that's already in your Mac. **It's perfect for a dead trackpad, but you can't type while it's on and it has no right-click key**, which is why people who use it daily look for an alternative.

> **Short answer:** Mouse Keys is a free, built-in macOS feature: turn it on in System Settings > Accessibility > Pointer Control > Mouse Keys, then move the pointer with `7` `8` `9` `U` `O` `J` `K` `L` and click with `I`. It works with no mouse or trackpad at all, so it's the right first step when one breaks. Its limits show up with daily use: you can't type while it's on, its page lists no right-click key, and it can't click a button by name. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) is the paid alternative for people who want the keyboard to be their mouse every day.

#### How to turn on Mouse Keys on a Mac

1. Choose **Apple menu > System Settings**, then click **Accessibility**.
2. Click **Pointer Control** and turn on **Mouse Keys**.
3. Click the **info button** next to Mouse Keys and turn on **Press the Option key five times to toggle Mouse Keys**. Now you can switch it on and off without opening Settings.
4. In the same options, set **Initial delay** and **Maximum speed** to taste.

No working pointer at all? Press `Option-Command-F5` (or triple-press Touch ID) to open the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, which can turn Mouse Keys on or off. The path above is the same in Apple's guides for macOS Sequoia 15 and Tahoe 26.

##### The Mouse Keys keys

| Action | Keyboard (no keypad) | Numeric keypad |
|---|---|---|
| Move the pointer | 7 8 9 U O J K L | 7 8 9 4 6 1 2 3 |
| Click | I | 5 |
| Press and hold (start a drag) | M | 0 |
| Release | . | . |

The movement keys sit in a ring around the click key (`I`, or keypad `5`), laid out like the numeric keypad.

#### Mouse Keys not working? Check these first

- **"My keyboard stopped typing."** That's Mouse Keys doing its job. Apple says: "When Mouse Keys is on, you can't use the keyboard or numeric keypad to enter text." Turn it off to type.
- **It turned itself off (or on).** If the Option-five-times option is set, pressing `Option` repeatedly while typing can toggle it by accident. Turn it back on the same way.
- **The arrow keys do nothing.** Mouse Keys doesn't use them. On a laptop, use `7` `8` `9` `U` `O` `J` `K` `L`.
- **The trackpad stopped working.** Check whether **Ignore built-in trackpad when Mouse Keys is on** is turned on in the Mouse Keys options.
- **The pointer is painfully slow.** Raise **Maximum speed** and lower **Initial delay**.

If the real problem is a mouse or trackpad that stopped responding, our [Mac trackpad not working](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working) guide walks through Apple's fixes, including turning Bluetooth on without a pointer.

#### Where Mouse Keys falls short

Mouse Keys is a good emergency tool and fine for the odd click. As a daily driver, its limits add up:

- **You can't type while it's on.** Every time you want to fill in a field, you toggle it off, type, and toggle it on again.
- **No right-click key.** Apple's Mouse Keys page lists none. For right-clicks you turn on Alternate pointer actions in the same settings pane, or use Voice Control. See [how to right-click without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/right-click-without-mouse-mac).
- **Fixed keys.** The options Apple lists are the Option toggle, ignoring the trackpad, initial delay and maximum speed. There's no setting to choose different movement keys.
- **No scrolling keys, middle click or back/forward** on Apple's page.
- **Aiming is slow.** To press a button across the screen, you steer the pointer all the way there. There are no labels and no grid.

macOS has other built-ins that help: [Full Keyboard Access](https://nomousemode.com/full-keyboard-access-mac) moves between controls with Tab, and Voice Control can label buttons by voice. Each fills one gap, but none is a complete keyboard mouse.

#### What No Mouse Mode does differently

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) starts where Mouse Keys stops:

- **Click buttons without aiming.** Press `⇧⌘Space` and every button, link, tab and menu in the front window, plus the menu bar and the Dock, gets a letter label. Type it and it's clicked. Or press `⇧⌘/` and type part of the button's name.
- **Movement that feels like a mouse.** `W` `A` `S` `D` move the cursor smoothly and speed up as you hold. Hold `Shift` to go fast or `Q` for one-pixel precision.
- **Every button.** `Space` clicks (twice to double-click, hold to drag), `Return` right-clicks, `M` middle-clicks, `[` and `]` go back and forward.
- **Scrolling.** Arrow keys scroll in every direction, and scroll areas (`⇧⌘J`) number each pane so you scroll the right one.
- **Reach anywhere fast.** `E` opens a 3×3 grid that zooms in with each press; two or three presses reach any spot, in any app.
- **Typing still works.** It also uses letter keys while it's on, but it switches itself off when you click into a text box, can stay off in apps you list, and has an optional hold-to-use mode (hold Right Command or Right Option). Shortcuts with Command, Control or Option always reach your app.
- **Your keys, your way.** Every key and shortcut can be remapped.

#### Mouse Keys vs No Mouse Mode at a glance

|  | Mouse Keys | No Mouse Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, built into macOS | $19.99 one time for 1 Mac (as of October 2026); no free trial |
| Movement keys | 7 8 9 U O J K L or keypad | W A S D (remappable), fast and precise modes |
| Click a button by label or name | No | Yes, labels and type to click |
| Right-click key | None listed (use Alternate pointer actions) | Return |
| Middle, back/forward | Not on Apple's page | Yes |
| Drag | Hold with M, release with . | Hold Space and move |
| Scrolling | Not on Apple's page | Arrow keys, numbered scroll areas |
| Grid to reach anywhere | No | Yes, 3×3 zooming grid |
| Typing while on | Not possible | Turns itself off in text boxes; hold-to-use option |
| Remap keys | No setting listed | Every key and shortcut |
| Works with no pointer device | Yes, nothing to install | Needs installing and setting up first |
| Requirements | Built into macOS | macOS 14 Sonoma or later, Apple silicon or Intel |

#### Which should you use?

- **Use Mouse Keys** if your trackpad or mouse just died, if you need a few clicks until a replacement arrives, or if you don't want to install anything. It's free and it's already there.
- **Use No Mouse Mode** if you want to work without a mouse every day, for comfort, [RSI](https://nomousemode.com/keyboard-only-mac-rsi) or speed, and you need to type, right-click and scroll without toggling things on and off.

The demo on this page uses the same keys as the app, so you can try the feel right now. For more ways to steer the pointer, see [how to move the mouse with the keyboard on a Mac](https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac), or compare every option in [the best keyboard mouse apps for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/best-keyboard-mouse-apps-for-mac).

**Mouse Keys, plus labels, right-click and a grid** No Mouse Mode moves the pointer with W A S D, clicks buttons by their labels and switches itself off when you click into a text box. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### How do I turn on Mouse Keys on a Mac?

Choose Apple menu > System Settings > Accessibility > Pointer Control, then turn on Mouse Keys. To toggle it from the keyboard later, click the info button next to Mouse Keys and turn on "Press the Option key five times to toggle Mouse Keys". You can also press Option-Command-F5 to open the Accessibility Shortcuts panel.

##### Which keys move the pointer with Mouse Keys?

On a keyboard without a numeric keypad: 7 8 9 U O J K L move the pointer, I clicks, M presses and holds the button, and the period (.) releases it. With a keypad: 7 8 9 4 6 1 2 3 move, 5 clicks, 0 holds and . releases.

##### Why can't I type after turning on Mouse Keys?

That's how Mouse Keys works. Apple says that when Mouse Keys is on, you can't use the keyboard or numeric keypad to enter text. Turn it off (press Option five times if you turned that option on) to type again.

##### How do I right-click with Mouse Keys?

Apple's Mouse Keys page lists no right-click key. For a right-click from the keyboard, turn on Alternate pointer actions in the same Pointer Control settings, or use Voice Control. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) right-clicks with Return. More options in [how to right-click without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/right-click-without-mouse-mac).

##### Why is Mouse Keys not working on my Mac?

Check that it's actually on (pressing Option five times toggles it if that option is set, so it's easy to switch off by accident). On a laptop, use 7 8 9 U O J K L, not the arrow keys. If the trackpad stopped responding instead, look for "Ignore built-in trackpad when Mouse Keys is on" in its options. If the pointer feels slow, change Initial delay and Maximum speed there.

##### Is No Mouse Mode a Mouse Keys app?

It does what Mouse Keys does and more. No Mouse Mode moves the pointer with W A S D, with fast and one-pixel precise modes, and adds click labels, type to click, right, middle and back/forward clicks, scrolling, a jump grid and remappable keys. It costs $19.99 one time for 1 Mac and needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later. There's no free trial; the site has in-browser demos.

### Shortcat vs No Mouse Mode: search to click, or the whole mouse

Source: https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-shortcat  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

Shortcat is a command palette for clicking: type what you want and it clicks it. **If clicking named buttons is all you need, Shortcat may be enough. If you also want to move the pointer, drag, scroll panes and reach things with no name, No Mouse Mode covers that.**

> **Short answer:** Shortcat is a free-download command palette for clicking: press `⇧⌘Space`, type the name of a button, and it clicks it. It's a 0.x beta, last updated in July 2025. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) ($19.99 one time, as of October 2026) also clicks by typing, either with letter labels or by name, and adds the rest of the mouse: smooth pointer movement, drag, middle and back/forward clicks, a jump grid and scroll areas. If you only click named buttons, try Shortcat first. If you want to leave the mouse in the drawer, No Mouse Mode covers more.

#### Two ways to click without a mouse

Both apps start from the same idea: macOS knows where the buttons are, so you shouldn't have to aim a pointer at them. They differ in how much of the mouse they replace.

- **Shortcat is search to click.** You open its palette, type what you want ("ok" finds an OK button), and it clicks it. After 2 seconds (configurable) it also shows black-on-yellow labels with 1 to 3 letter shortcuts.
- **No Mouse Mode is a keyboard mouse.** It has two ways to click by typing (labels and type to click), plus a mode where your keys *are* the mouse: `W` `A` `S` `D` move the pointer, `Space` clicks, `Return` right-clicks and the arrow keys scroll.

So the question is whether you need to click things, or do everything a mouse does.

#### What Shortcat does well

[Shortcat](https://shortcat.app) describes itself as "the universal command palette for your Mac". From its site and docs (as of October 2026):

- **Type what you see.** It indexes the interface and you search by name. That's natural if you already live in a launcher or command palette.
- **More than a left click.** Right-click, double-click and clicks with modifier keys.
- **Extras:** window search, menu search and an emoji mode.
- **Broad app support:** Safari, Chrome, Firefox, some Chromium browsers and most Electron apps. Its own docs add that "effectiveness may vary depending on application's Accessibility implementation."
- **Easy to get:** a free download, or `brew install shortcat`. The official site states no price. It needs macOS 13 or later and runs on Apple silicon and Intel.

##### What to know before you rely on it

Shortcat is still a 0.x beta. The latest version is v0.12.2, from July 3, 2025, and the one before it, v0.12.1, moved the beta expiry date out to 2030. There have been long gaps before: before April 2025, the previous release was in January 2023. That doesn't mean it has stopped working, and plenty of people use it happily. It just means you can't count on regular updates the way you might with a paid, actively released app.

#### What No Mouse Mode adds

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) 2.0 is a menu bar app that turns the keyboard into a mouse. The clicking side will feel familiar to Shortcat users:

- **Click labels** (`⇧⌘Space`): every button, link, tab and menu in the front window, plus the menu bar and the Dock, gets letter labels. Type one to click it. Hold `Shift` with the last letter to right-click, `Command` to Command-click, `Option` to double-click or `Control` to just move the pointer there. `Tab` keeps labels open for several clicks, and a window's labels stay the same each time, so they become muscle memory.
- **Type to click** (`⇧⌘/`): type part of a button's or text's name. Case, spaces and accents don't matter, and initials work ("nf" finds New Folder). `Return` clicks. This is the closest match to Shortcat's search.

Then it covers what search-to-click doesn't:

- **A real pointer.** Press `⇧⌘M` and `W` `A` `S` `D` glide the cursor with eased movement. Hold `Shift` for speed or `Q` for one-pixel precision. That matters for things that aren't buttons: a spot on a canvas, a slider, the edge of a window.
- **Every mouse button.** Click, double, triple, drag (hold `Space`), right, middle, and back/forward with `[` and `]`.
- **Jump grid** (`E`): a 3×3 grid labelled Q W E / A S D / Z X C that zooms in with each press. Two or three presses reach anywhere, in any app, whether or not it describes its buttons to macOS.
- **Scroll areas** (`⇧⌘J`): each scrollable pane gets a number. Pick one, then scroll with the arrows or `J`/`K`, page with `Space`, or jump to the top or bottom with `T`/`B`.
- **Saved spots and display jumps.** Save up to nine cursor positions, jump back with ```, and move between displays with `Tab`.
- **A way in for awkward apps.** Some apps don't tell macOS where their buttons are, so labels (in any app that relies on that, Shortcat included) find little. No Mouse Mode can optionally read on-screen text with Apple's on-device text recognition to label those apps too. It needs Screen Recording permission, and nothing is saved or sent. Buttons that are only icons still need the grid or W A S D.

It's easy to learn: setup is guided, a Practice window has nine hands-on lessons, and `H` shows every key. Every key and shortcut can be remapped.

#### Shortcat vs No Mouse Mode at a glance

|  | Shortcat | No Mouse Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Approach | Command palette: search to click, labels after a delay | Click labels, type to click, plus a keyboard-driven pointer |
| Default shortcut | ⇧⌘Space | ⇧⌘Space labels, ⇧⌘/ type to click, ⇧⌘J scroll areas, ⇧⌘M on/off |
| Right, double, modifier clicks | Yes | Yes, plus triple, middle, back/forward |
| Move the pointer freely | Not among its listed features | Yes, W A S D with fast and precise modes |
| Drag | Not among its listed features | Yes, hold Space |
| Grid for any spot on screen | Not among its listed features | Yes, 3×3 zooming grid |
| Scroll a chosen pane | Not among its listed features | Yes, numbered scroll areas |
| Window and menu search, emoji | Yes | No (labels cover the menu bar and Dock) |
| Apps without accessibility info | "Effectiveness may vary" | Optional on-device text recognition; grid and W A S D work everywhere |
| macOS | 13+, Apple silicon and Intel | 14 Sonoma or later, Apple silicon and Intel |
| Latest release | v0.12.2 beta, July 2025 | 2.0.1 |
| Price (as of October 2026) | Free download; no price on its site | $19.99 one time for 1 Mac; no free trial |

#### Who should pick which

##### Pick Shortcat if…

- you mostly click buttons and links that have a name, and still reach for the trackpad now and then;
- you like a search box more than labels;
- you want window search and menu search in the same tool;
- you'd rather not pay, and you're fine with a beta that was last updated in July 2025.

##### Pick No Mouse Mode if…

- you want to stop using the mouse or trackpad, not just use it less, for comfort, a [broken trackpad](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working) or [RSI](https://nomousemode.com/keyboard-only-mac-rsi);
- you need to drag, select text, hit unlabeled spots or [move the pointer with the keyboard](https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac);
- you scroll a lot in multi-pane apps like mail, chat or code editors;
- you want one app with a guided setup and a practice window, and a current, maintained release.

If you're still weighing up label apps, [No Mouse Mode vs Homerow](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-homerow) and [Homerow alternatives](https://nomousemode.com/homerow-alternatives) cover Shortcat's closest neighbour.

#### Can you run Shortcat and No Mouse Mode together?

Yes. Some people keep Shortcat for its menu and window search and use No Mouse Mode for the pointer, grid and scrolling. The one thing to sort out is the shortcut, because **both default to `⇧⌘Space`**. (Homerow's site demos show the same combination, so this isn't unusual.) In No Mouse Mode:

1. Click the No Mouse Mode icon in the menu bar and choose **Settings…**.
2. Open the **General** tab and find **Anywhere shortcuts**.
3. Click the **Click labels** field and press the new shortcut you want.

You can also skip the global shortcut: while No Mouse Mode is on, plain `F` opens click labels and `/` opens type to click. Shortcuts that use Command, Control or Option always reach the app in front, so they keep working while No Mouse Mode is on.

#### The bottom line

Shortcat is a clever, free-download way to click by name, and if that's the only mouse job you want to replace, it's worth a try. No Mouse Mode is for people who want the whole mouse on the keyboard: clicking by label or name, a smooth pointer, drag, a grid for anywhere on screen and pane-by-pane scrolling. The demo on this page uses the same keys as the app, so you can feel the difference before you [buy](https://nomousemode.com/#pricing). For the full field, see the [best keyboard mouse apps for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/best-keyboard-mouse-apps-for-mac).

**Click by typing, then keep going without a mouse** No Mouse Mode gives you click labels, type to click, smooth W A S D movement, a jump grid and scroll areas in one menu bar app. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### What is Shortcat for Mac?

Shortcat calls itself "the universal command palette for your Mac". It indexes the buttons and other elements on screen, and you type what you want to click, such as "ok" for an OK button. It also does right-clicks, double-clicks, clicks with modifier keys, window search, menu search and an emoji mode. Its default shortcut is `⇧⌘Space`.

##### Is Shortcat free?

Shortcat is a free download from its site or with `brew install shortcat`, and its official site lists no price as of October 2026. It is still a 0.x beta; version 0.12.1 moved its beta expiry date to 2030.

##### Is Shortcat still maintained?

Its latest release is v0.12.2 from July 3, 2025, so as of October 2026 it was last updated in July 2025. Before the 2025 releases, the previous one was v0.11.4 in January 2023. It still runs on macOS 13 and later; its docs say it was tested on macOS 15.3.

##### Shortcat vs Homerow: which is better?

They overlap a lot: both put keyboard labels on buttons and both let you search. Homerow is $49.99 one time (as of October 2026), is free to try with a reminder every 50 activations, needs macOS 13 or later and had releases in March 2026. Shortcat is a free-download beta last updated July 2025. See [No Mouse Mode vs Homerow](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-homerow) for how Homerow compares with us.

##### Can I use Shortcat and No Mouse Mode together?

Yes, but both use `⇧⌘Space` by default, so change one. In No Mouse Mode, open the menu bar icon, choose Settings…, go to General and record a new Click labels shortcut under Anywhere shortcuts. You can also press `F` for labels while No Mouse Mode is on.

##### Does No Mouse Mode have a free trial?

No. No Mouse Mode is $19.99 one time for 1 Mac, with free updates. Instead of a trial, the [website](https://nomousemode.com/) has interactive in-browser demos that use the same keys as the app.

### How to right-click on a Mac without a mouse

Source: https://nomousemode.com/right-click-without-mouse-mac  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

**With a trackpad, hold Control and click.** With no pointer at all, use Alternate pointer actions, Voice Control, the Contextual Menu key on some Apple keyboards, or No Mouse Mode, where Return right-clicks.

> **Short answer:** Apple calls a right-click a **secondary click or Control-click**. If your trackpad works, **hold Control and click**. With no working pointer, macOS offers **Alternate pointer actions** (keyboard shortcuts for right-click) and **Voice Control**, and some Apple keyboards have a **Contextual Menu key**. Mouse Keys alone has no right-click key. In [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/), **Return** right-clicks where the pointer is, and **⇧ with a label's last letter** right-clicks that button.

#### 1. Control-click (needs a trackpad or mouse)

The classic. Hold `Control` and click with the trackpad or mouse, and the shortcut menu opens. It's the right answer if your trackpad works but you don't have a two-button mouse.

##### Change how the trackpad right-clicks

Open System Settings → **Trackpad** (or **Mouse**) and use the **Secondary click** pop-up menu to choose how a right-click works on that device. If clicks aren't registering at all, see [what to do when your Mac trackpad isn't working](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working).

#### 2. The Contextual Menu key

On the **Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad (USB-C)**, the Contextual Menu key, below F13, opens a shortcut menu. It's the closest thing to a dedicated right-click key on an Apple keyboard.

#### 3. Alternate pointer actions (built in, keyboard only)

Mouse Keys moves the pointer with `7` `8` `9` `U` `O` `J` `K` `L` and clicks with `I`, but Apple's Mouse Keys page lists no right-click key. For that, turn on **Alternate pointer actions**:

1. Open System Settings → **Accessibility → Pointer Control**.
2. Turn on **Alternate pointer actions**.
3. Assign a keyboard shortcut to right-click. It also covers left-click, double-click and drag and drop, and can use switches or facial expressions instead of keys.

Pair it with Mouse Keys to get the pointer where you want it first. Remember that Mouse Keys blocks typing while it's on. More on that in [how to move the mouse with the keyboard](https://nomousemode.com/move-mouse-with-keyboard-mac).

#### 4. Voice Control

Turn on System Settings → Accessibility → **Voice Control**. Say "Show numbers" to label what's on screen, then say a command with the item's number. Apple's [Voice Control commands](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/use-voice-control-commands-mh40719/mac) page lists them. For spots without a label, "Show grid" puts a numbered grid over the screen and saying a number zooms in. "Hide numbers" and "Hide grid" put them away.

#### 5. No Mouse Mode: right-click from the keyboard

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) gives you right-click in every one of its modes, so you never have to set it up separately.

- **At the pointer:** press `⇧⌘M` to turn it on, move with `W` `A` `S` `D`, and press `Return` to right-click.
- **On a button:** press `⇧⌘Space` for click labels, then hold `⇧` while typing the label's last letter. The button is right-clicked without moving the pointer by hand.
- **By name:** press `⇧⌘/`, type part of the button's or text's name, and press `⇧Return`.
- **Anywhere on screen:** press `E` for the jump grid, pick cells until you're on target, then press Return.

When the menu opens, the arrow keys and Return pick an item. Labels depend on apps describing their buttons to macOS, which most do. The jump grid and W A S D work in any app.

#### All the ways compared

| Method | Needs a pointer device? | Setup | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control-click | Yes | None | Working trackpad, one-button mouse |
| Contextual Menu key | No | Needs that specific keyboard | Owners of the Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad (USB-C) |
| Alternate pointer actions + Mouse Keys | No | Two settings and a shortcut | Occasional right-clicks, free |
| Voice Control | No | Turn on, learn commands | Hands-free use |
| No Mouse Mode | No | Install, allow Accessibility | Frequent right-clicks from the keyboard, $19.99 one time for 1 Mac (as of October 2026) |

#### Which one should you use?

- **Trackpad works, no second button:** Control-click. Nothing to set up.
- **Trackpad or mouse is dead right now:** Alternate pointer actions with Mouse Keys, or Voice Control. Both are free and built in. If your Bluetooth mouse simply dropped, Apple's tip is to press `⌘Space`, type Bluetooth File Exchange, press Return, then Return again to turn Bluetooth on. More fixes in [Mac trackpad not working](https://nomousemode.com/mac-trackpad-not-working).
- **You right-click many times a day without touching the trackpad:** a keyboard app saves the most time, because the right-click is one key and you can aim at a button by its label instead of steering.

#### Other clicks you'll need

Right-click is rarely the only thing a trackpad does for you. Here's how the same tools handle the rest.

- **Double-click:** Alternate pointer actions has a double-click action. In No Mouse Mode, press Space twice, or hold `⌥` with a label's last letter.
- **Drag:** in Mouse Keys, `M` presses and holds and `.` releases. In No Mouse Mode, hold Space and move with W A S D.
- **Command-click (new tab):** in No Mouse Mode, hold `⌘` with a label's last letter.
- **Middle click and back / forward:** No Mouse Mode uses `M`, `[` and `]`.

Every No Mouse Mode key can be remapped in Settings if Return doesn't suit you as the right-click key.

#### Right-click, step by step with No Mouse Mode

1. Press `⇧⌘M` to turn No Mouse Mode on.
2. Move to the item with `W` `A` `S` `D` (hold Shift for speed), or press `E` and pick grid cells.
3. Press `Return` to right-click.
4. Or skip the pointer: press `⇧⌘Space` and hold `⇧` as you type a label's last letter.
5. Pick from the menu with the arrows and Return.

Right-click is one piece of going mouse-free. The full picture is in [how to use a Mac without a mouse](https://nomousemode.com/how-to-use-mac-without-mouse), and if you're comparing tools, see [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys) or [the best keyboard mouse apps for Mac](https://nomousemode.com/best-keyboard-mouse-apps-for-mac).

**Right-click any button from the keyboard** In No Mouse Mode, Return right-clicks where the pointer is, and Shift with a label's last letter right-clicks that button. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### What is the keyboard shortcut for right-click on a Mac?

macOS has no single right-click key on most keyboards. Holding Control while you click does it with a trackpad or mouse. The Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad (USB-C) has a Contextual Menu key. For a keyboard shortcut you set up yourself, turn on Alternate pointer actions in System Settings → Accessibility → Pointer Control. In [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/), Return right-clicks.

##### How do I right-click on a MacBook trackpad?

Hold Control and click. To choose how secondary click works on the trackpad itself, open System Settings → Trackpad and use the Secondary click pop-up menu.

##### Can Mouse Keys right-click?

Apple's Mouse Keys page lists no right-click key. Its keys are I to click, M to press and hold, and the period to release. For right-click, turn on Alternate pointer actions in the same Pointer Control settings.

##### How do I right-click with Voice Control?

Turn on Voice Control in System Settings → Accessibility → Voice Control, say "Show numbers" to label what's on screen, then give a command for the numbered item. Apple's Voice Control command list has the full set.

##### How do I right-click a specific button without moving the pointer?

In [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/), press Shift-Command-Space to show click labels, then hold Shift while you type the label's last letter. In type to click (Shift-Command-/), Shift-Return right-clicks the match.

### Vimac alternatives: what to use now that Vimac is Homerow

Source: https://nomousemode.com/vimac-alternative  
Updated: 2026-10-31 · Author: Ahmed Gagan (maker of No Mouse Mode)

Vimac, the free open-source app that became Homerow, hasn't been updated since 2022. **Homerow is its official successor; No Mouse Mode, Shortcat, Scoot, Wooshy and macOS's own tools are the other options.**

> **Short answer:** Vimac is no longer developed. Its README says "Vimac is now Homerow", and its last code change was on December 31, 2022. If you want the direct successor, that's [Homerow](https://www.homerow.app) ($49.99 once, free to try). If you want Vimac's hint labels and scroll mode plus a full keyboard mouse, try [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) ($19.99 once for one Mac). Scoot is the free, open-source pick. Shortcat and Wooshy suit people who'd rather type a button's name, and macOS's built-in tools are free.

#### What happened to Vimac?

[Vimac](https://github.com/nchudleigh/vimac) was a free, open-source (GPL-3.0) app for "keyboard-driven navigation" on macOS, with about 3,690 GitHub stars. Its README now says:

- **"Vimac is now Homerow"**, described as "a refined, sleeker, more performant successor of Vimac."
- The **last commit was December 31, 2022**. There are no GitHub releases.
- The repository isn't archived, but nothing has changed since. vimacapp.com didn't respond when we checked in October 2026, and we found no Homebrew cask.

So if Vimac is acting up on your Mac, or you're wondering whether it's safe to keep relying on it, the honest answer is that no fixes are coming. It's time to pick a maintained replacement.

#### What Vimac users miss

Vimac had two modes, and most people switching want both back:

##### Hint mode

Hold Space (the default) and hint text appears on the elements in the frontmost window. Type a hint to click, double-click or right-click that element.

##### Scroll mode

A red border marks the active scroll area, and H J K L scroll it, Vim style.

The rest of this page maps those two modes onto each option available today.

#### How each option maps to Vimac

As of October 2026. "Not listed" means the app's own site or README doesn't mention it.

| App | Like hint mode | Like scroll mode | Price | Maintained? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Homerow | Labels, plus search | Scroll mode | $49.99 once, free to try | Yes, 1.5.3 (March 2026) |
| **No Mouse Mode** | Click labels, plus type to click | Scroll areas, J/K to scroll | $19.99 once (1 Mac), no trial | Yes, 2.0.1 |
| Shortcat | Type to search; labels after 2 seconds | Not listed | Free download (no price on site) | Last updated July 2025 (beta) |
| Scoot | Element mode in the focused window | Can scroll | Free, open source | Yes, v1.3 (March 2026) |
| Wooshy | Type to search and click | Not listed | Free with naps; $3.88/mo or $46.28/yr | Yes |
| macOS built-ins | Voice Control "Show numbers" | Not a dedicated mode | Free | Part of macOS |

#### Homerow: the official successor

[Homerow](https://www.homerow.app) is the app Vimac's README points to. Its site shows labels, search and scroll, and version 1.1.0 added extra scroll-mode commands. It's actively maintained (1.5.3 came out in March 2026) and needs macOS 13 or later.

The big change for Vimac users is price: Homerow is **$49.99 once**, covering all your personal Macs and future updates, and it isn't open source. It's free to try, with a reminder every 50 activations. If you liked Vimac and just want it modernised, this is the natural next step. Our [Homerow vs No Mouse Mode comparison](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-homerow) has the full feature table.

#### No Mouse Mode: Vimac's two modes, plus a keyboard mouse

[No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) covers both Vimac modes and then fills the gaps that hint labels leave.

- **Hint mode → click labels.** `⇧⌘Space` labels every button, link, tab and menu, including the menu bar and the Dock. Type the letters to click. Hold Shift with the last letter to right-click or Option to double-click, just like Vimac's hint actions, or Command for a Command-click. Labels for a window stay the same each time.
- **Scroll mode → scroll areas.** `⇧⌘J` numbers each scrollable pane. Pick one, then J and K scroll, Space pages, and T / B jump to the top or bottom.
- **Type to click.** `⇧⌘/` lets you type part of a button's name instead of a hint (initials work).

Beyond that, press `⇧⌘M` and the keyboard becomes a mouse: W A S D move the pointer smoothly, Space clicks or drags, Return right-clicks, and the arrow keys scroll. `E` opens a 3×3 jump grid that reaches anywhere in two or three presses, even in apps with no labels. An optional on-device text recognition mode adds labels in apps that don't describe their buttons to macOS. Every key can be remapped, and a Practice window with nine lessons gets you fluent.

**Trade-offs:** there's no free trial (the site has interactive demos with the same keys), all sales are final, it isn't open source, and it needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later.

#### Scoot: the free, open-source option

If Vimac's open-source license mattered to you, [Scoot](https://github.com/mjrusso/scoot) is the closest in spirit. It's BSD-3-Clause and updated in March 2026. `⇧⌘J` shows labels on buttons and links in the focused window, which is close to Vimac's hint mode. `⇧⌘K` adds a grid across your screens and `⇧⌘L` a freestyle mode where you nudge the cursor with macOS, Emacs or vi text shortcuts. It can move, click, drag and scroll.

Its README says it runs on macOS 11 and 12 and doesn't mention newer versions, so try it on your Mac before you rely on it. Note that its `⇧⌘J` default is the same as No Mouse Mode's scroll areas shortcut; both apps let you change it.

#### Shortcat and Wooshy: type the name instead

If you'd rather type what you see than learn hint letters, two apps are built around search.

- **[Shortcat](https://shortcat.app)** is a command palette: press `⌘⇧Space`, type "ok" to click an OK button. After two seconds it shows one- to three-letter labels, so it also works a bit like hint mode. It supports right, double and modifier clicks, and window and menu search. It's a 0.x beta, last updated July 2025, and a free download. See [No Mouse Mode vs Shortcat](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-shortcat).
- **[Wooshy](https://wooshy.app)** searches the whole interface, including the Dock and menu bar, and clicks. The free version "takes some random naps"; a subscription ($3.88 a month or $46.28 a year) keeps it running all the time. It needs macOS 14.6.

Neither lists a scroll mode, so you'd scroll with the keyboard the usual way.

#### macOS built-ins: free, if slower

- **Voice Control** is the closest built-in to hint mode: say "Show numbers", then "Click" and a number. "Show grid" adds a numbered grid.
- **Full Keyboard Access** lets you Tab between controls and press Space. See our [Full Keyboard Access guide](https://nomousemode.com/full-keyboard-access-mac).
- **Mouse Keys** moves the pointer with keys, but you can't type text while it's on. Compared in [No Mouse Mode vs Mouse Keys](https://nomousemode.com/no-mouse-mode-vs-mouse-keys).

#### Which one should a Vimac user pick?

- **You want Vimac, but maintained:** Homerow.
- **You want hint and scroll modes plus pointer movement, dragging and a grid:** [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/).
- **You want free and open source:** Scoot.
- **You'd rather type names than hints:** Shortcat or Wooshy.
- **You need something right now at no cost:** Voice Control or Full Keyboard Access.

Came to Vimac from the browser? Read [Vimium for the whole Mac](https://nomousemode.com/vimium-for-mac). For the full field, see [Homerow alternatives](https://nomousemode.com/homerow-alternatives).

**Hint labels and scroll mode, still maintained** No Mouse Mode is $19.99 once for one Mac, with free updates and no subscription. Price and checkout: https://nomousemode.com/#pricing ($19.99 one-time for 1 Mac, free updates; macOS 14+ on Apple silicon and Intel).

#### FAQ

##### Is Vimac dead?

Effectively, yes. Vimac's last code change was on December 31, 2022, it has no GitHub releases, and its README says "Vimac is now Homerow". The repository isn't archived, but no one is updating it. When we checked in October 2026, vimacapp.com didn't respond.

##### Why is Vimac not working on my Mac?

We can't say for certain what's wrong on your Mac. What we do know is that Vimac hasn't been updated since 2022, so problems that show up on newer macOS versions won't get fixes. First check that it still has Accessibility permission in System Settings. If it still doesn't work, it's time to move to a maintained app.

##### Is Homerow the same as Vimac?

Homerow is Vimac's successor. Vimac's README calls it "a refined, sleeker, more performant successor of Vimac." Unlike Vimac, Homerow is a paid app ($49.99 once as of October 2026, free to try) and isn't open source.

##### Is there a free, open-source Vimac alternative?

Scoot is free and open source (BSD-3-Clause) and was updated in March 2026. It has a label mode for buttons in the focused window, a grid mode and a freestyle pointer mode. Its README only says it runs on macOS 11 and 12, so test it on your version.

##### Which Vimac alternative has a scroll mode?

Homerow has a scroll mode. [No Mouse Mode](https://nomousemode.com/) has scroll areas (`⇧⌘J`): each pane gets a number, then J/K scroll, Space pages and T/B jump to the top or bottom. Scoot can scroll too.

##### Can I still download Vimac?

The source code is still on GitHub under GPL-3.0, but there are no GitHub releases and we found no Homebrew cask. Because it's unmaintained, we'd suggest one of the maintained options on this page instead.
